messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Miguel Alvarez is a 67-year-old physician who has spent most of his career in hospital medicine, and he speaks about the months surrounding his daughter’s life-threatening illness as if they exist in fragments rather than as a story. He can place certain scenes with painful clarity—the fluorescent wash of the pediatric ICU at 3 a.m., the sound of monitors alarming, the sight of her skin turning gray while staff rushed around the bed—but between those moments there are blanks he cannot bridge. He says he knows what happened, yet when he tries to describe it, the words disappear. He starts a sentence, stops, presses his fingers to his mouth, and says it is as if he only has pieces and cannot make them hold together long enough to tell himself what occurred from beginning to end.

At the time, Miguel was still working full-time as a doctor, moving between patient rooms and charting stations while his daughter’s condition worsened. What made the ordeal especially piercing was how familiar the medical setting was; he understood enough to recognize the danger in each change of vital signs, each urgent exchange among the ICU team, each code cart rolling past. Now the hospital itself has become densely charged. A monitor tone on his unit, the smell of antiseptic, or seeing a parent standing rigidly at a child’s bedside can abruptly pull him out of the present. In those moments he feels a surge of fear and horror and, for an instant, reacts as if he is back there again watching his daughter slip away. He has become constantly watchful, scanning rooms and hallways before he even realizes he is doing it.

Because the memory comes to him in these jagged, wordless flashes, Miguel has worked hard not to think about it at all. He says that if he lets his mind go near those ICU nights, he will get trapped in images he cannot organize or explain. He avoids any deliberate reflection on that period and keeps himself occupied almost continuously—taking extra charting home, staying late to review labs, leaving the television on in the background, filling quiet hours with tasks so there is no opening for his mind to drift. The less coherent the memory feels, the more determined he becomes to push it away.

The same is true when the sense of danger rises in the present. After a flashback on the ward triggered by a child crying behind a curtain, Miguel spent the rest of the shift rigid and overalert, listening for every alarm and feeling ashamed by how shaken he was. He has come to dread those surges of fear, and in response he tries to shut the whole subject down immediately. If a colleague mentions a critically ill child, he redirects the conversation. If an image of the ICU appears in his mind while driving home, he turns on sports radio and concentrates on traffic. He believes staying busy is the only way to keep himself from being overwhelmed.

Over time, these habits have narrowed his life and, paradoxically, left the worst moments less settled. Because he repeatedly cuts off his thoughts and distracts himself whenever the memory begins to form, the experience remains disjointed. He still cannot tell a clear story, even privately, and this seems to intensify his conviction that the event is too much to face directly. He notices that what returns are the same isolated sensory shards—the alarm, the pale face, the compressed panic in the room—rather than a fuller account with a beginning and end.

His constant efforts to suppress and outwork the memories have also left him more on edge. The more he monitors himself for signs that a flashback might be coming and the more quickly he tries to force thoughts away, the more easily ordinary hospital cues ignite a fresh wave of alarm. He has become superalert at work in a way his colleagues have started to notice: pausing at monitor sounds, lingering outside pediatric rooms, tensing when family members look frightened. Although he continues to function professionally, he now rearranges parts of his day to minimize exposure when he can, asking others to step in on certain cases and burying himself in administrative tasks whenever possible.

Miguel finally sought help after realizing that even outside the hospital he was never really off duty inside his own mind. A siren near a grocery store parking lot recently brought on such a vivid sense of being back in the ICU that he had to grip the shopping cart until it passed. What frightened him most was not only the intensity of the reaction, but the feeling that after all this time he still cannot put the experience into words or rest. He says he wants, more than anything, to be able to remember what happened to his daughter without feeling as if he is back in the worst minute of it, and he is afraid that if nothing changes, the hospital—the place that has defined his whole adult life—will remain a place of constant threat.
